title: Accountants and auditors
claude_rationale: Accounting work is predominantly digital and cognitive, involving data analysis, financial reporting, and compliance checking - all areas where AI tools are already making significant impact by automating routine tasks like data entry, basic calculations, and standard report generation. However, the profession requires regulatory compliance, client interaction, strategic advisory work, and professional judgment that AI cannot fully replace. Demand elasticity is moderate because while cheaper accounting services could expand access for small businesses and enable more frequent financial analysis, growth is constrained by regulatory requirements, business formation rates, and the fact that most entities already have mandatory accounting needs. The occupation will survive but require substantial skill shifts toward advisory, analytical, and strategic roles as routine tasks become automated.
opus_rationale: Core accounting and auditing work — examining financial records, computing taxes, analyzing data, identifying risks, preparing reports — is overwhelmingly digital and cognitive, putting it directly in AI's path; routine tasks like data entry, reconciliation, and document review are already being automated by AI and RPA tools. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper, faster financial analysis unlocks some latent demand (more small businesses get proper advisory services, more granular analysis, more frequent auditing), but core demand is structurally capped by regulatory requirements, the fixed number of entities needing audits, and the fact that compliance needs don't multiply with lower cost. The combination of very high disruption with moderate elasticity means the occupation persists but shifts decisively toward advisory, judgment, and client-facing roles while routine preparation work shrinks, requiring workers to substantially upskill — the hallmark of restructuring rather than wholesale replacement.
openai_rationale: AI is already impacting accountants and auditors by automating routine tasks such as data entry and basic financial analysis, allowing professionals to focus more on advisory and analytical roles. This results in a high disruption score as AI tools become more integrated into their workflows. However, the demand elasticity is moderate because while AI can enhance productivity, the need for human judgment in complex decision-making and compliance with evolving regulations remains significant. Thus, the occupation will likely restructure, with a shift towards more strategic and consultative roles, requiring adaptation by the workforce.
gpt55_rationale: Accounting and auditing are heavily digital, rules-based, document-centered, and analytical, making many tasks such as transaction coding, reconciliations, tax preparation, audit sampling, anomaly detection, and report drafting highly exposed to AI and automation. However, the occupation still requires professional judgment, regulatory accountability, client communication, audit signoff, and interpretation of ambiguous business situations, so AI is more likely to transform workflows than eliminate the role outright. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper accounting can unlock more advisory services, better controls, and higher-quality analysis for small businesses and individuals, but many core needs such as annual audits, tax filings, and compliance cycles are structurally limited. This fits a restructure outcome: routine production work shrinks while accountants who can supervise AI, validate outputs, manage risk, and provide strategic advice remain valuable.

title: Actors
claude_rationale: AI significantly disrupts acting through deepfakes, digital doubles, voice synthesis, and virtual performers that can handle certain roles, especially background work, commercials, and some lead roles in digital media. However, the core human elements of live performance, authentic emotional expression, and audience connection remain largely irreplaceable. Demand elasticity is moderate - while cheaper digital actors could expand content creation in some areas (like personalized content, indie films, or interactive media), traditional entertainment demand is somewhat constrained by audience attention and cultural factors, though new formats may emerge.
opus_rationale: Acting's core involves physical, embodied performance and the human appeal of recognizable performers, which AI cannot fully replicate, but AI is encroaching on voiceover, background/extra work, digital doubles, and synthetic media — pushing disruption to a moderate level. Demand for content is somewhat elastic as cheaper production unlocks more video and media, but the value of human celebrity and live performance caps how much AI productivity translates into more human acting work. Because the disruption score sits at or below 6 and the human-presence core remains intact, the occupation is best categorized as resilient, with AI eroding certain subfields (extras, voiceover) rather than reshaping the central craft.
openai_rationale: AI can potentially disrupt the acting profession by generating digital characters or enhancing visual effects, but the core of acting involves human creativity, emotional expression, and physical presence, which are difficult for AI to fully replicate. Thus, the disruption is moderate. Demand elasticity is moderate as well; while AI could make production cheaper and faster, the unique appeal of human actors and the limited capacity for audiences to consume more content restricts massive demand expansion. Overall, the occupation is resilient, as AI will augment rather than replace the human element in acting.
gpt55_rationale: Acting has an embodied, interpersonal, and live-performance component that AI cannot fully replicate, especially in theater, theme parks, and high-status screen roles. However, a large share of recorded-media work—voiceover, dubbing, extras, commercials, background performances, synthetic avatars, and some low-budget screen acting—is directly exposed to generative audio and video tools, making disruption high. Demand could expand as cheaper production enables more ads, games, training videos, localization, and niche entertainment, but audience attention, celebrity economics, union rules, and preference for human performers limit how much of that expansion becomes employment for actors. The occupation is therefore likely to be substantially restructured, with more value placed on distinctive human performance, likeness rights, live work, and hybrid AI-production skills.

title: Actuaries
claude_rationale: Actuaries work primarily with data analysis, statistical modeling, and risk assessment - all core AI capabilities that are rapidly advancing. AI can already perform sophisticated statistical analysis, pattern recognition in large datasets, and predictive modeling that forms the foundation of actuarial work. However, demand for actuarial services is relatively inelastic because insurance needs are largely fixed by regulatory requirements, population demographics, and existing business structures - companies don't suddenly need 10x more risk assessments just because they become cheaper to produce. The combination of high AI disruption potential with constrained demand expansion suggests significant headcount reduction as AI tools enable fewer actuaries to handle the same workload.
opus_rationale: Actuarial work is predominantly digital and cognitive—statistical modeling, data analysis, forecasting, and report generation—which are squarely in AI's path, driving a high disruption score. However, demand elasticity is low because the volume of insurance products, regulatory filings, and risk assessments is structurally and regulatorily constrained; cheaper actuarial output does not unlock dramatically more demand, and certification requirements gate the role rather than expand its scope. While BLS projects strong nominal growth, AI productivity gains are likely to compress per-task headcount needs, so the combination of high disruption and limited demand expansion fits the replace category, though strong projected growth and the heavy communication/judgment component may soften the contraction toward restructuring.
openai_rationale: Actuaries primarily engage in knowledge work involving statistical analysis, risk assessment, and financial modeling, which AI can assist with but not fully automate due to the complexity and need for human judgment. AI tools can enhance efficiency in data analysis and modeling, but the core tasks still require human oversight and decision-making. Demand elasticity is low because the need for actuarial services is driven by regulatory and industry-specific requirements, which do not expand proportionally with cost reductions. Thus, while AI will augment actuaries' capabilities, it is unlikely to significantly reduce headcount, making the occupation resilient.
gpt55_rationale: Actuarial work is highly digital and analytical: compiling data, building statistical models, pricing products, calculating reserves, writing reports, and explaining results are all tasks that AI can substantially accelerate. Human actuaries will still be needed for regulatory accountability, professional judgment, assumptions governance, and communication with executives and regulators, but much of the junior and mid-level modeling, coding, documentation, and scenario analysis is directly exposed. Demand for actuarial analysis may expand somewhat as firms model more risks, personalize insurance products, and use enterprise risk management more broadly, but insurance regulation, required sign-offs, and the limited number of pricing/reserving decisions constrain expansion. Because disruption is high and elasticity is relatively low, productivity gains are likely to reduce the number of actuaries needed for many routine analytical functions, even if senior credentialed roles remain important.

title: Administrative services and facilities managers
claude_rationale: Administrative services and facilities managers have moderate disruption potential as AI can assist with data analysis, scheduling, compliance monitoring, and some administrative tasks, but the core work requires physical oversight of facilities, staff management, and real-world problem-solving that demands human presence and judgment. Demand elasticity is low because organizations have relatively fixed needs for facility management and administrative oversight - making these services 10x cheaper wouldn't cause companies to dramatically expand their office space or administrative infrastructure. Since disruption is at the boundary (6) but doesn't reach the high threshold of 7+, this occupation falls into the resilient category where AI enhances some tasks but doesn't fundamentally reshape the role.
opus_rationale: The role mixes significant knowledge work (records management, procurement analysis, scheduling, compliance documentation) that AI can streamline with substantial physical-presence and human-coordination duties — supervising maintenance staff, monitoring buildings, handling on-call emergencies, and managing renovation projects. AI will automate the administrative and recordkeeping portions but cannot replace the oversight of physical facilities and people management, capping disruption at moderate. Demand is structurally tied to the number of buildings and organizations needing management rather than to cost suppression, so productivity gains mostly reduce per-manager workload rather than unlocking large latent demand, yielding low elasticity. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes peripheral tasks but not the core supervisory and facilities-oversight work.
openai_rationale: Administrative services and facilities managers engage in a mix of tasks, including supervision, compliance, and maintenance oversight, which are not easily automated by AI. While AI can assist with data management and operational efficiency, the core tasks require human judgment and presence. Demand elasticity is moderate; while AI could enhance efficiency, the need for human oversight in compliance and facility management limits dramatic demand expansion. Thus, the occupation is resilient, with AI augmenting but not replacing core functions.
gpt55_rationale: AI will materially change the administrative, records, compliance, procurement, scheduling, reporting, and energy-analysis portions of this occupation, and AI-enabled building systems can support predictive maintenance and monitoring. However, much of facilities management still requires onsite judgment, vendor coordination, staff supervision, emergency response, inspections, and accountability for safety and regulatory compliance in physical spaces. Demand elasticity is limited because organizations do not need dramatically more facilities management simply because it becomes cheaper; demand is tied to the number, size, and complexity of buildings and organizations. Because disruption is significant but not high enough to fully reshape the physical and managerial core of the job, the occupation fits the resilient category.

title: Adult basic and secondary education and ESL teachers
claude_rationale: AI significantly disrupts the knowledge-work portions of teaching through personalized learning platforms, automated assessment, and adaptive curriculum delivery, but core human elements like cultural sensitivity, motivation, and one-on-one support remain essential. Demand elasticity is high because adult education is currently constrained by cost and accessibility - AI-powered tools could dramatically expand access to basic education, ESL instruction, and GED preparation for underserved populations globally. While AI will transform how these teachers work, the massive latent demand for affordable adult education means employment could grow despite productivity gains.
opus_rationale: The core work involves in-person instruction, motivating adult learners, cultural sensitivity, and adapting to diverse abilities — tasks requiring human presence and interpersonal judgment that AI cannot fully replace, though AI tutoring tools materially assist lesson planning, language practice, and individualized instruction, placing disruption at the moderate-to-high boundary. Demand has some latent elasticity since cheaper personalized language and literacy instruction could expand access, but structural factors like declining enrollment, government funding constraints, and the social/motivational nature of these classroom programs cap that growth at moderate. Because the disruption score lands at 6 — AI augments planning and practice but does not reshape the human-centered core of teaching adult learners — this occupation fits the resilient category rather than restructure.
openai_rationale: AI can assist adult education and ESL teachers by providing tools for personalized learning, language translation, and progress tracking, which moderately disrupts the occupation. However, the core tasks of teaching, adapting to individual student needs, and cultural sensitivity require human interaction and judgment, limiting AI's impact. Demand elasticity is low because the number of adults seeking basic education or ESL services is not significantly suppressed by cost, and societal factors like high school graduation rates and government funding heavily influence demand. Thus, the occupation is resilient, with AI augmenting rather than replacing teachers.
gpt55_rationale: Much of this occupation is language-based and cognitive: lesson planning, explaining concepts, grading, progress monitoring, individualized practice, and ESL conversation support are all areas where AI tutors and adaptive learning tools are already useful. However, teachers still provide motivation, classroom management, cultural sensitivity, assessment of nonacademic barriers, and connections to community resources, which keeps disruption below the most automatable digital occupations. Demand could expand because cheaper personalized instruction would help adults who cannot attend scheduled classes or afford tutoring, especially ESL learners, but growth is limited by public funding, student time constraints, credentialing needs, and declining adult education enrollment. The result is a substantial shift in the teacher role toward facilitation, coaching, assessment, and support rather than straightforward replacement, so the net effect is restructure.

title: Advertising sales agents
claude_rationale: Advertising sales involves predominantly cognitive tasks like client research, proposal creation, presentation development, and relationship management that AI can increasingly automate or significantly enhance. AI tools already assist with lead generation, personalized outreach, proposal writing, and market analysis. The elasticity is low because advertising budgets are typically fixed or constrained by business revenue - companies don't dramatically increase advertising spend just because sales processes become more efficient. The existing 6% projected decline in employment reflects structural shifts toward automated digital ad placement, confirming that productivity gains won't translate to expanded demand for human sales agents.
opus_rationale: The work is predominantly digital and language-based — prospecting, drafting proposals, preparing reports, analyzing sales statistics, and ad placement — much of which is already being automated by programmatic ad-buying platforms and AI-assisted CRM/outreach tools, driving high disruption. Demand elasticity is low: advertising budgets are constrained by client revenue and marketing spend, and the shift to automated programmatic ad placement directly removes the human intermediary rather than expanding the need for agents, as reflected in the BLS -6% projection. Productivity gains accrue to platforms and tools rather than unlocking dramatically more human-sold ad inventory. With disruption at 7 and elasticity at 4, headcount contraction is the expected outcome, fitting the replace category.
openai_rationale: Advertising sales agents face high disruption as AI and digital tools increasingly automate tasks like client targeting, ad placement, and performance analysis. The shift towards digital advertising reduces the need for traditional sales roles. Elasticity is low because while digital advertising is growing, it doesn't require a proportional increase in sales agents due to automation efficiencies. Thus, the net effect is 'replace' as AI absorbs core tasks and demand does not expand sufficiently to maintain headcount.
gpt55_rationale: Advertising sales agents perform highly language- and information-based work: prospecting, writing outreach, preparing pitches, generating proposals, recommending ad formats, maintaining CRM records, and analyzing account performance. AI and automated ad platforms can already handle much of lead generation, campaign recommendation, proposal drafting, reporting, and self-service ad placement, although human relationship-building and complex negotiations remain important for larger accounts. Demand for advertising is not fixed, but it is constrained by client budgets, available attention, and measurable ROI; cheaper sales support may help small advertisers somewhat but will not create proportionate demand for human agents. Because disruption is high and elasticity is relatively low, AI is likely to reduce headcount while leaving a smaller group focused on strategic relationship management and complex accounts.

title: Advertising, promotions, and marketing managers
claude_rationale: Marketing and advertising managers face high disruption as AI transforms core tasks like market research, campaign optimization, content creation, and data analysis - areas that are predominantly digital and cognitive. AI tools already materially assist with audience targeting, A/B testing, creative generation, and performance analytics. However, demand elasticity is high because cheaper, faster, and more precise marketing capabilities unlock significant latent demand - small businesses can access sophisticated marketing previously available only to large corporations, and the explosion of digital channels creates more opportunities for targeted campaigns. The net effect is augmentation as productivity gains enable each manager to handle more campaigns and clients rather than reducing headcount.
opus_rationale: Marketing management is predominantly knowledge work—campaign planning, content strategy, market analysis, copy generation, ad placement, and audience segmentation are all directly in AI's path, with generative AI and automated ad platforms already materially changing daily workflows. However, marketing demand is highly elastic: cheaper and faster content production, personalization, and analytics unlock vastly more campaigns, channels, micro-segments, and continuous optimization that were previously cost-prohibitive. Because productivity gains expand the total volume of marketing output rather than simply reducing headcount, demand absorbs the disruption, and the managerial layer (strategy, judgment, client relationships, brand stewardship) remains essential to direct AI tools. This fits 'augment'—each manager produces far more output while overall employment stays stable or grows.
openai_rationale: Advertising, promotions, and marketing managers are highly susceptible to AI disruption due to the digital and cognitive nature of their work, such as data analysis, campaign planning, and market research. AI tools are already enhancing these tasks by providing insights and automating routine processes. However, the demand for these roles is likely to expand as AI makes marketing campaigns more efficient and cost-effective, unlocking new opportunities and markets. This combination of high disruption and high elasticity suggests that while the skill set may evolve, overall demand for these managers will grow, leading to an 'augment' net effect.
gpt55_rationale: This occupation is heavily cognitive, digital, and language-based: market research, campaign planning, audience segmentation, pricing analysis, copy and creative evaluation, media optimization, and reporting are all areas where AI tools are already materially useful. However, the role also includes client relationships, cross-functional coordination, negotiation, budget accountability, brand judgment, and staff management, which keep it from being fully automatable. Demand has moderate elasticity because cheaper marketing enables more personalization, experimentation, and access for smaller firms, but total demand is limited by consumer attention, firm budgets, and the need for accountable human decision-makers. The best fit is restructure: AI will substantially change workflows and reduce demand for some routine campaign and analysis tasks, while increasing the value of managers who can use AI strategically and oversee more complex marketing systems.

title: Aerospace engineering and operations technologists and technicians
claude_rationale: While AI can assist with data analysis, computer simulations, and some design optimization tasks, the core work involves hands-on installation, calibration, and maintenance of physical aerospace equipment and test facilities. The occupation requires significant physical presence for assembly work, equipment operation, and safety monitoring that AI cannot replace. Demand elasticity is low because aerospace testing and manufacturing requirements are driven by regulatory compliance and safety standards rather than cost considerations - even if AI made certain tasks faster, the number of aircraft designs and required testing procedures wouldn't dramatically increase. The disruption score of 6 places this in the resilient category where AI augments but doesn't fundamentally reshape the core work.
opus_rationale: The core work involves substantial physical, hands-on tasks—building and maintaining test facilities, installing parts and instruments in aircraft, calibrating wind tunnels, and assembly—that require real-world presence and cannot be automated by AI. AI does meaningfully assist the digital portions (running computer simulations, recording and analyzing test data, programming test equipment), pushing disruption to a moderate level, but the manual and on-site safety-critical work anchors the role. Demand elasticity is moderate-to-high because cheaper satellite launches, drones, and new aircraft types are expanding the aerospace sector, suggesting productivity gains would be absorbed by more testing and production rather than headcount cuts. With disruption at or below 6, the occupation is best classified as resilient—AI augments the analytical periphery but the physical core endures.
openai_rationale: The role of aerospace engineering and operations technologists and technicians involves a mix of physical and cognitive tasks, such as installing and maintaining equipment, which are not easily automated by AI. While AI can assist with simulations and data analysis, the hands-on nature of the work limits disruption. Demand elasticity is moderate; while AI could enhance productivity, the demand for aerospace innovations like small satellites and drones suggests some expansion potential. Thus, the occupation is resilient, with AI augmenting rather than replacing core tasks.
gpt55_rationale: AI will materially affect the analytical and digital parts of this job, including test-data analysis, simulation setup, calibration diagnostics, documentation, and troubleshooting recommendations. However, the core work still involves physical test facilities, instrumentation, aircraft or spacecraft hardware, safety procedures, and hands-on installation and maintenance that require human presence in controlled environments. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper testing and analysis could support more satellite, drone, electric aircraft, and aerospace R&D projects, but growth is limited by capital intensity, regulation, safety certification, and physical testing bottlenecks. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to displace the hands-on core of the occupation, the net effect is resilient.

title: Aerospace engineers
claude_rationale: Aerospace engineering involves substantial digital design work, simulation, analysis, and optimization that AI can significantly enhance - from aerodynamic modeling to structural analysis to systems integration. However, the work requires deep domain expertise, safety-critical decision making, and integration with physical testing and manufacturing processes that maintain human oversight requirements. Demand elasticity is moderate because while AI-accelerated design could enable more aerospace projects and faster innovation cycles (especially in emerging areas like small satellites and drones), the industry is heavily regulated, capital-intensive, and constrained by physical testing requirements and certification processes. The combination of high disruption to core technical tasks but moderate demand expansion due to regulatory and capital constraints places this in the restructure category, where engineers who adapt to AI-augmented workflows will thrive while those who don't may be displaced.
opus_rationale: Aerospace engineering is predominantly knowledge work centered on design, simulation, analysis, and computational modeling — all directly in AI's path, with generative design, automated CFD/FEA optimization, and AI-assisted testing already reshaping workflows, driving a high disruption score. However, the work also requires physical prototyping, regulatory compliance, security-cleared defense work, and team coordination that anchor a human role. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, faster design unlocks meaningful latent demand in expanding markets like small satellites, drones, and commercial space, but growth is capped by capital intensity, safety regulation, and the limited number of major aerospace programs. Disruption >=7 with elasticity of 6 places this in restructure — the occupation persists and grows modestly, but skill sets shift toward AI-augmented design and systems integration, displacing engineers who don't adapt.
openai_rationale: Aerospace engineering involves a significant amount of knowledge work, including design, analysis, and testing, which can be enhanced by AI tools. AI can assist in simulations, design optimizations, and predictive maintenance, but human oversight and creativity remain crucial, especially in safety-critical and innovative tasks. Thus, disruption is high but not maximal. The elasticity score is high because advancements in AI could reduce costs and increase the speed of aerospace development, potentially unlocking new markets and increasing demand for aerospace products, such as drones and small satellites. Therefore, the net effect is 'augment' as productivity gains are likely to be absorbed by increased demand.
gpt55_rationale: Aerospace engineering is heavily computer-based and cognitive, involving modeling, simulation, requirements analysis, design review, documentation, and troubleshooting, all of which AI can significantly accelerate. However, the work remains tied to physical systems, safety certification, testing, manufacturing constraints, and multidisciplinary accountability, so AI is unlikely to fully absorb the occupation. Demand would expand as cheaper engineering enables more satellite, drone, defense, propulsion, and aircraft redesign projects, but growth is limited by capital costs, regulation, testing cycles, and procurement bottlenecks. This fits a restructure outcome: core workflows and skill requirements change substantially, but demand and real-world constraints prevent simple replacement.

title: Agricultural and food science technicians
claude_rationale: AI significantly disrupts the analytical and data processing aspects of this work - sample analysis, test result compilation, report generation, and pattern recognition in crop/food data are all areas where AI tools are already proving valuable. However, the physical components (sample collection, equipment operation, laboratory maintenance) and the need for hands-on expertise in agricultural/food systems remain important. Demand elasticity is high because cheaper, faster agricultural and food testing could unlock significant latent demand - more frequent soil testing, expanded food safety monitoring, broader crop disease surveillance, and enhanced quality control across smaller operations that currently can't afford comprehensive testing services.
opus_rationale: The work mixes physical hands-on tasks—collecting and preparing samples, operating lab and farm equipment, inspecting food in processing plants—with cognitive tasks like analyzing test results and preparing reports. AI can assist with the data analysis and reporting portions, but the core requires physical presence in labs, farms, and processing plants for sample collection, equipment operation, and inspection, which keeps disruption moderate. Demand could expand modestly as cheaper analysis enables more agricultural research and quality control, but it is structurally tied to regulatory testing requirements and physical throughput rather than unlimited latent demand. Since disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI augments the analytical periphery but does not reshape the fundamentally physical, presence-dependent core work.
openai_rationale: Agricultural and food science technicians perform a mix of physical and cognitive tasks, including sample collection, equipment operation, and data analysis. AI can assist with data analysis and reporting, but the hands-on nature of sample collection and equipment operation limits disruption to moderate levels. Demand elasticity is moderate as productivity gains could lead to more extensive research and testing, but structural and regulatory factors may limit expansion. Overall, the occupation is resilient, with AI augmenting some tasks but not fundamentally reshaping the role.
gpt55_rationale: This occupation combines hands-on sample collection, lab preparation, equipment operation, field or plant work, and sterile/safety procedures with cognitive tasks such as recording results, analyzing data, and writing reports. AI can meaningfully improve the analytical and documentation portions, including anomaly detection, image-based disease identification, experiment tracking, and report generation, but much of the core work still requires physical presence in labs, farms, processing plants, and greenhouses. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper testing and analysis could lead to more frequent food safety checks, soil testing, crop monitoring, and agricultural R&D, especially under climate and supply-chain pressures, though regulation, budgets, and physical sampling needs limit unlimited expansion. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, AI is more likely to augment workflows and change tools than to fundamentally replace the occupation.

title: Agricultural and food scientists
claude_rationale: Agricultural and food scientists face high disruption as AI can significantly enhance their core knowledge work including data analysis, research design, genetic analysis, and predictive modeling for crop yields and food safety. However, the work still requires substantial fieldwork, laboratory experimentation, and physical sample collection that AI cannot replace. Demand elasticity is high because cheaper and faster agricultural research could unlock massive latent demand - more crops could be optimized, more food safety testing conducted, and personalized nutrition solutions developed at scale, especially as global food security challenges intensify. The combination of high disruption with high elasticity suggests workers will become dramatically more productive while total demand expands.
opus_rationale: The work mixes substantial cognitive components (data analysis, experiment design, literature review, modeling crop/animal genetics) where AI is already materially useful, with significant physical and field-based requirements (lab experiments, farm visits, sample collection, biosecurity compliance) that AI cannot perform. This blend places disruption at moderate (5) — AI accelerates analysis and hypothesis generation but cannot replace the hands-on empirical core. Elasticity is moderate (6) because cheaper, faster research could unlock more agricultural innovation given pressing demands around climate, pests, water resources, and food safety, though regulatory validation and physical experimentation cap expansion. Because disruption is at or below 6, the occupation is classified resilient: AI reshapes the analytical periphery but the empirical, field-bound core work remains intact.
openai_rationale: Agricultural and food scientists engage in a mix of fieldwork and laboratory research, with significant portions of their tasks involving data analysis, research, and communication, which are increasingly supported by AI tools. AI can enhance productivity in data analysis and experimental design, but the physical aspects and the need for human judgment in research remain significant. The demand for agricultural innovation is high due to challenges like climate change and food security, suggesting that productivity gains from AI could lead to increased research output rather than reduced headcount. Therefore, while AI will disrupt the occupation by enhancing productivity, the demand elasticity is high enough to absorb these gains, leading to an 'augment' net effect.
gpt55_rationale: Agricultural and food scientists do substantial knowledge work—literature review, experimental design, statistical analysis, modeling, technical writing, regulatory documentation, and product or breeding optimization—that AI can materially accelerate. However, much of the occupation still depends on laboratory experiments, field trials, biological growth cycles, food-processing constraints, inspections, and hands-on implementation, so AI is unlikely to fully automate the role. Demand has moderate elasticity because cheaper research could expand work on climate resilience, food safety, crop productivity, sustainable inputs, and new food products, but demand is constrained by regulation, validation requirements, capital equipment, and biological timelines. Because disruption is high but demand expansion is only moderate, the occupation is best categorized as restructure: scientists will remain needed, but workflows and required skills will shift strongly toward AI-enabled data science, automation, and model-guided experimentation.

title: Agricultural engineers
claude_rationale: Agricultural engineers face high disruption as their core work involves computer-aided design, data analysis, systems optimization, and integration of AI/geospatial technologies - all areas where AI tools are rapidly advancing and already providing material assistance. The elasticity is high because cheaper, faster agricultural engineering solutions can unlock massive latent demand globally - more efficient farming systems, precision agriculture, and automated technologies become accessible to smaller operations and developing regions when costs drop dramatically. Despite the high disruption, the combination of growing global food security needs and AI-enabled cost reductions suggests demand expansion will absorb productivity gains, leading to augmentation rather than replacement.
opus_rationale: A meaningful portion of the work is digital and cognitive—CAD design, systems modeling, data analysis, and integrating AI/geospatial systems—which AI tools materially accelerate, but the core role still requires substantial physical presence at farms, labs, and construction sites, plus hands-on oversight of equipment and facilities, capping disruption at moderate. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper, faster engineering could unlock more precision-agriculture and automation projects as farmers seek cost reductions, but the field is small and constrained by capital-intensive agricultural cycles and slow adoption. Since disruption is 6 (below the 7 threshold) and the physical, multi-stakeholder nature of the work limits full automation, the occupation is best classified as resilient—AI reshapes the design and analysis periphery but does not displace the integrated engineering role.
openai_rationale: Agricultural engineers engage in a mix of digital and physical tasks, such as designing systems using software and overseeing construction operations. AI can assist in design and analysis, but the need for human oversight in physical environments remains significant. The disruption score reflects AI's potential to enhance design and analysis tasks but not fully replace the human element. Demand elasticity is moderate; while AI could make agricultural engineering more efficient, the demand for these services is not heavily suppressed by cost, limiting dramatic expansion. Thus, the occupation is resilient, with AI augmenting rather than replacing core tasks.
gpt55_rationale: Agricultural engineers do substantial cognitive and digital work—CAD design, modeling, simulation, data analysis, and increasingly AI/geospatial integration—so AI will meaningfully change workflows and raise productivity. However, the occupation remains tied to physical equipment, farms, facilities, environmental conditions, testing, construction oversight, safety, and licensed engineering judgment, which limits full automation of the core role. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper engineering could accelerate precision agriculture, automation, irrigation, biofuels, and environmental compliance projects, but adoption is constrained by farm capital budgets, regulation, and the physical pace of implementation. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to fully reshape or replace the occupation, the net effect is resilient.

title: Agricultural workers
claude_rationale: Agricultural work remains predominantly physical and hands-on, requiring real-world presence for tasks like planting, harvesting, animal care, and equipment operation in unpredictable outdoor environments. While AI may assist with some record-keeping and equipment automation, the core work of crop cultivation and livestock management requires human dexterity, physical strength, and adaptability to weather and biological systems. Demand for agricultural products is relatively inelastic - people don't consume dramatically more food if production becomes cheaper, and regulatory/biological constraints limit how much productivity gains can expand total agricultural employment. The occupation shows resilience as AI touches only peripheral aspects while core physical tasks remain human-dependent.
opus_rationale: Core tasks are overwhelmingly physical—planting, harvesting, herding, feeding livestock, operating machinery in unpredictable outdoor conditions—which AI software cannot perform directly. Disruption comes mainly from physical automation (robotic harvesters, automated tractors) rather than AI cognitive tools, and these mechanization gains shift work toward equipment operators rather than eliminating the occupation through AI. Demand for agricultural output is relatively inelastic since food consumption is fairly fixed and productivity gains historically reduce labor headcount rather than expand it. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is resilient to AI in the language/cognitive sense, even though it faces slow employment decline from physical mechanization.
openai_rationale: Agricultural workers primarily engage in physical tasks such as planting, harvesting, and tending to livestock, which are less susceptible to AI disruption. While AI and automation can assist with machinery operation and data tracking, the core tasks remain largely manual and hands-on. The elasticity score reflects limited potential for demand expansion; while mechanization can increase productivity, the demand for agricultural products is not highly elastic and is constrained by market and consumption limits. Thus, the net effect is 'resilient' as AI impacts are peripheral rather than transformative.
gpt55_rationale: Most agricultural worker tasks are physical, outdoor, and variable—planting, harvesting, feeding, herding, cleaning, repairing, and handling animals or crops—so current AI alone cannot perform the core job without substantial robotics and machinery. AI-enabled precision agriculture, autonomous tractors, robotic harvesters, sensors, and advanced irrigation will change some workflows and reduce some manual labor, especially in large-scale crop production, but adoption will be uneven across crops, farms, and regions. Demand elasticity is low because food demand is constrained by population, diets, land, water, and biological growing cycles, so cheaper labor does not lead consumers to buy many times more agricultural output. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate rather than primarily digital or AI-substitutable, the occupation fits the resilient category despite gradual mechanization-driven employment pressure.

title: Air traffic controllers
claude_rationale: Air traffic control involves significant cognitive work (monitoring radar, making quick decisions, coordinating multiple aircraft) that AI could potentially assist with, but the core responsibility requires real-time human judgment for safety-critical decisions in unpredictable situations with human lives at stake. The work is heavily regulated and requires immediate physical presence in control towers and facilities. Demand for air traffic control is essentially fixed by the number of flights and airports - even if AI made controllers 10x more efficient, we wouldn't suddenly have 10x more air traffic, and safety regulations would likely maintain minimum staffing requirements regardless of technological capabilities.
opus_rationale: Air traffic control is heavily cognitive and data-driven, and AI/automation systems like NextGen already increase per-controller capacity, suggesting meaningful disruption to workflow. However, the core work involves real-time, life-safety decision-making under strict regulatory accountability where full automation is socially and legally constrained, keeping humans firmly in the loop and capping disruption at moderate. Demand is highly inelastic — the number of flights to coordinate is fixed by air traffic volume, not by the cost or speed of control services, so productivity gains translate into modestly more traffic handled per controller rather than expanded demand. Because disruption stays at or below 6 and the role's safety-critical human-in-the-loop nature is durable, this occupation is resilient.
openai_rationale: Air traffic control involves a mix of digital and cognitive tasks, such as monitoring radar screens and communicating with pilots, which AI can assist with but not fully automate due to the need for real-time decision-making and human judgment in unpredictable situations. AI can enhance efficiency by aiding in data analysis and traffic prediction, but human oversight remains crucial for safety. Demand elasticity is low because the number of flights is not highly sensitive to the cost of air traffic control; thus, productivity gains from AI are unlikely to significantly increase the number of controllers needed. Overall, while AI may augment certain tasks, the core responsibilities and demand for human controllers remain stable, making the occupation resilient to AI disruption.
gpt55_rationale: Air traffic control is highly cognitive, real-time, and screen/radio-mediated, with core tasks such as monitoring aircraft, detecting conflicts, sequencing traffic, and issuing clearances all in the path of advanced automation and AI decision-support systems. However, safety certification, liability, and the need for human oversight in abnormal situations will slow full substitution, so the disruption score is high but not maximal. Demand elasticity is low because the number of controllers needed is tied mainly to flight volumes, airport capacity, and regulation; cheaper controller labor would not cause society to fly several times more. Given high disruption and low elasticity, AI-enabled productivity would mostly reduce staffing needs over time rather than unlock enough new demand to offset displacement.

title: Aircraft and avionics equipment mechanics and technicians
claude_rationale: This occupation scores low on disruption because the core work is predominantly hands-on physical maintenance, repair, and inspection of aircraft components that requires direct manipulation of mechanical systems, working in uncomfortable positions, and real-world problem-solving with safety-critical equipment. While AI might assist with some diagnostic data interpretation or maintenance scheduling, the fundamental tasks of physically repairing engines, replacing parts, and conducting safety inspections cannot be automated. Elasticity is low because aircraft maintenance demand is largely fixed by regulatory requirements, fleet size, and flight hours - even if AI made diagnostics faster, the same number of aircraft still need the same physical maintenance cycles. The net effect is resilient because AI touches only peripheral aspects like documentation or diagnostic assistance while leaving the core mechanical work unchanged.
opus_rationale: The core work is hands-on physical repair, inspection, and maintenance of aircraft requiring dexterity, physical strength, and in-person presence in hangars and on airfields — tasks largely outside AI's direct reach. AI may assist with diagnostics, predictive maintenance scheduling, and interpreting test data, but these are peripheral aids that don't replace the manual labor or FAA-regulated certification requirements. Demand is structurally tied to fleet size and flight hours and is heavily constrained by safety regulation, so productivity gains wouldn't dramatically expand the volume of physical maintenance needed. With disruption well below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI touches the periphery while the regulated, physical core remains intact.
openai_rationale: Aircraft and avionics equipment mechanics and technicians perform tasks that are predominantly physical and hands-on, such as repairing and inspecting aircraft components, which limits the impact of AI on their core tasks. While AI can assist with diagnostics and maintenance scheduling, the physical nature of the work and strict regulatory requirements mean disruption is low. Demand elasticity is also low because the need for maintenance is driven by the number of aircraft and regulatory requirements, not cost. Thus, even if AI increases productivity, it won't significantly expand demand. The occupation remains resilient due to the essential and regulated nature of the work.
gpt55_rationale: AI can materially assist the diagnostic and documentation portions of this occupation, including troubleshooting avionics faults, interpreting maintenance manuals, analyzing sensor data, and generating records. However, the core work remains hands-on, safety-critical, site-specific repair, inspection, installation, and testing of physical aircraft systems under FAA certification requirements, so AI is unlikely to absorb most daily tasks within 10 years. Demand is only modestly elastic because maintenance is tied to fleet size, flight activity, and regulatory schedules rather than discretionary consumption, though cheaper diagnostics and reduced downtime could support some additional aviation activity. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate and the physical, regulated core persists, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Airline and commercial pilots
claude_rationale: While AI assists with flight planning, weather analysis, and navigation systems, the core piloting tasks remain fundamentally physical and require real-time human judgment for safety-critical decisions, emergency response, and aircraft control. Current autopilot technology handles routine flight phases but pilots must actively monitor systems and take control during takeoffs, landings, and emergencies. Demand elasticity is low because air travel is largely driven by economic factors and route capacity rather than pilot costs, and regulatory requirements mandate human pilots for passenger safety. The occupation remains resilient as AI enhances existing systems rather than replacing the essential human oversight role.
opus_rationale: While modern aircraft are heavily automated and AI can enhance flight planning, autopilot, and systems monitoring, the core work of piloting requires physical presence in the cockpit, real-time judgment in emergencies, and—critically—deep regulatory and safety/liability constraints that mandate certified human pilots for the next decade and beyond. Passenger trust and FAA certification requirements make full autonomy implausible within 10 years, so AI touches only the periphery (planning, monitoring, copilot assistance). Demand for air travel is moderately elastic—cheaper operations could expand routes and frequency—but pilot headcount per flight is regulated and unlikely to compress significantly. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient: AI augments tools but does not reshape the fundamental human-in-the-loop nature of flying.
openai_rationale: The core tasks of airline and commercial pilots involve significant physical presence and real-time decision-making, such as navigating aircraft and responding to changing conditions, which are not easily automated by AI. While AI can assist with flight planning and monitoring, the critical role of pilots in ensuring safety and managing emergencies limits disruption to peripheral tasks. Demand elasticity is low because the number of flights is primarily driven by passenger and cargo demand, which is not highly sensitive to reductions in pilot costs. Thus, AI's impact on this occupation is limited, making it resilient.
gpt55_rationale: Piloting already relies heavily on automation, and AI can further improve flight planning, weather/routing decisions, system monitoring, communications support, and simulator training. However, the core job still requires certified human responsibility in a safety-critical, regulated, real-world environment involving takeoff, landing, emergencies, passenger trust, and coordination with ATC and crew. Demand would expand only modestly if pilot labor became cheaper because air travel is constrained by aircraft, fuel, airport capacity, regulation, and the fact that people do not take 10x more flights simply because cockpit labor is cheaper. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to remove the human-centered core over the next decade, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Animal care and service workers
claude_rationale: Animal care work is fundamentally physical and hands-on, requiring direct interaction with living animals for feeding, grooming, exercising, and monitoring health - tasks that AI cannot perform. While AI might assist with peripheral administrative tasks like scheduling or record-keeping, the core work of animal handling, physical care, and real-time behavioral assessment remains entirely human-dependent. Demand shows moderate elasticity as lower costs could expand access to services like pet grooming, training, and boarding, but the physical nature of the work means productivity gains from AI would be minimal. The low disruption score keeps this occupation in the resilient category despite moderate demand elasticity.
opus_rationale: The core work — feeding, grooming, bathing, exercising, and physically handling unpredictable live animals — is almost entirely hands-on physical labor requiring real-world presence, compassion, and tactile skill that AI cannot perform. AI touches only peripheral tasks like scheduling, record-keeping, and behavior monitoring. Demand is moderately elastic, growing with pet ownership and willingness to spend, but it is constrained by the physical nature of the service rather than cost or speed of cognition. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient.
openai_rationale: Animal care and service work is predominantly physical and hands-on, involving tasks such as feeding, grooming, and exercising animals, which are not easily automated by AI. The disruption score is low because AI's role is limited to peripheral tasks like scheduling or record-keeping. However, the demand elasticity is moderate as the pet care industry is growing, driven by increasing pet ownership and willingness to spend on pet services. While AI may enhance efficiency, the core tasks require human interaction, making the occupation resilient to AI disruption.
gpt55_rationale: The core work is hands-on, physical, and location-specific: feeding, cleaning, grooming, exercising, observing, restraining, and training live animals in unpredictable real-world settings. AI can help with scheduling, customer communication, recordkeeping, remote monitoring, behavior notes, and some automated feeders or cleaning tools, but it does not replace the central human-animal interaction or physical care. Demand is moderately elastic because cheaper pet care, grooming, boarding, and training could lead owners to buy more services, especially as pets are increasingly treated as family members, but demand is still constrained by the number of pets and the need for trusted in-person care. title: Announcers and DJs
claude_rationale: AI disruption is high because core tasks like voice synthesis, music selection, content research, and script writing are directly in AI's path - AI DJs and automated programming already exist and are improving rapidly. The work is predominantly digital/cognitive rather than requiring physical presence. Demand elasticity is low because radio listening time and event hosting needs are relatively fixed - people don't consume dramatically more DJ services just because they're cheaper, and many stations are already moving toward automated programming to cut costs rather than expand content.
opus_rationale: The occupation is split: broadcast announcers and radio DJs do predominantly digital/voice-based work that AI voice synthesis can already replicate, and stations are explicitly adopting AI DJs, but party DJs and emcees (40% of the field) require physical presence at live events that AI cannot replace. This dual nature pulls the disruption score to moderate rather than high. Elasticity is low because demand for radio airtime and live event hosting is structurally capped—cheaper AI announcing does not meaningfully expand the number of weddings, clubs, or radio slots needing a host. Because disruption sits at 6, with the live-event segment insulated and even growing, the occupation overall is resilient even as the broadcast subsegment contracts.
openai_rationale: AI is increasingly capable of performing tasks such as selecting music, providing commentary, and even conducting interviews, which are core tasks for announcers and DJs. This leads to a high disruption score as AI tools can already assist significantly in these areas. However, the demand elasticity is moderate because while AI can make these services cheaper and more accessible, the unique human element of live performance and interaction still holds value, especially for DJs at live events. The net effect is 'restructure' as the occupation will need to adapt to AI integration, with a shift in skills towards leveraging AI tools and focusing on human-centric aspects of the role.
gpt55_rationale: A large share of broadcast announcing and radio DJ work is language-, audio-, and software-based: writing scripts, reading copy, selecting music, producing segments, doing promos, and engaging audiences online, all of which AI voice, generative writing, recommendation, and automation tools can already affect. Live event DJs and emcees are more resilient because they require physical presence, crowd reading, client interaction, and real-time social performance, but even there playlists, mixing, planning, and announcements can be partially automated. Demand elasticity is low because radio airtime, local advertising budgets, weddings, clubs, and events do not expand dramatically just because announcing or music hosting becomes cheaper. Given high disruption and limited ability for demand to absorb productivity gains, the occupation is likely to see replacement pressure, especially in broadcast and radio.

title: Anthropologists and archeologists
claude_rationale: AI moderately disrupts anthropology/archaeology through tools for data analysis, pattern recognition in artifacts, and research assistance, but core work remains fundamentally human-centered - fieldwork, cultural interpretation, and contextual understanding of human behavior require physical presence and nuanced judgment. opus_rationale: The work mixes significant digital/cognitive components (data analysis, report writing, literature synthesis, GIS, linguistic and pattern analysis) that AI materially assists with, but core tasks require fieldwork, physical excavation, in-person observation, interviews, and on-site regulatory compliance assessment that AI cannot perform. Demand is largely fixed by research funding, federal preservation regulations, and limited corporate market-research budgets, so cheaper analysis would not dramatically expand the number of excavations or studies undertaken. Because disruption is only moderate (5) — AI touches the analytical periphery but not the irreducible field-based core — the occupation is resilient, with stable modest growth driven by regulatory needs rather than productivity-driven contraction.
openai_rationale: The disruption score is moderate because while AI can assist with data analysis and pattern recognition, much of the work involves fieldwork, cultural understanding, and human interaction that AI cannot fully replicate. The elasticity score is low because the demand for anthropologists and archeologists is not heavily suppressed by cost; it is more constrained by funding and the specific nature of the work. The net effect is 'resilient' as AI will augment some tasks but not fundamentally change the core nature of the work, and demand is not expected to expand significantly with increased productivity.
gpt55_rationale: AI can substantially assist the digital and cognitive parts of this occupation, including literature review, transcription and translation, qualitative coding, GIS/remote-sensing analysis, artifact classification, database management, and report drafting. title: Arbitrators, mediators, and conciliators

opus_rationale: The work involves document analysis, applying rules and precedent, and preparing settlement agreements—all knowledge-based tasks AI can assist with—but the core function is facilitating trust, emotionally charged human negotiation, and rendering legitimate, often legally binding decisions that require neutral human authority and presence. Demand is somewhat constrained by the structural reality that arbitration/mediation volume is tied to existing disputes, regulatory mandates, and government budgets rather than being heavily price-suppressed. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI touches the analytical periphery but does not reshape the fundamentally interpersonal and authority-based core work.
openai_rationale: The core tasks of arbitrators, mediators, and conciliators involve facilitating communication and negotiation, which are predominantly cognitive and language-based. Demand elasticity is moderate because while AI could make dispute resolution more efficient, the demand for such services is not heavily suppressed by cost, and legal or procedural constraints limit rapid expansion. Thus, the occupation is resilient, with AI augmenting rather than replacing the human role.
gpt55_rationale: The occupation is heavily language-, document-, and judgment-based: AI can help review evidence, summarize claims, draft settlement language, research rules or precedents, and model possible resolutions. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper dispute resolution could unlock more low-value, consumer, workplace, family, and small-business disputes that are currently too costly to mediate, but total demand is constrained by the number of disputes, court or contract rules, public budgets, and parties’ willingness to accept AI-mediated outcomes. Because disruption is high but demand expansion is not strong enough to fully offset productivity gains, the occupation is likely to be restructured rather than broadly replaced or augmented.

title: Architects

opus_rationale: Much of an architect's work — design iteration, CADD/BIM modeling, drawing production, code research, cost estimation, and specifications — is digital and cognitive, putting it squarely in AI's path; generative design and AI-assisted BIM already materially change workflows, driving a high disruption score. gpt55_rationale: Architects do substantial digital and cognitive work—CAD/BIM drawings, specifications, code research, cost estimates, design iteration, renderings, and documentation—that AI and generative design tools can materially accelerate. Demand could expand as cheaper architectural services make custom design, renovations, sustainability upgrades, and more design iterations accessible to more clients, but total demand is constrained by construction budgets, permitting, land use rules, and the fact that architecture is only one part of project cost. This points to restructuring: fewer hours spent on drafting and routine documentation, more emphasis on design direction, client management, code/liability oversight, and construction-process coordination.

openai_rationale: Architectural and engineering managers are involved in planning, directing, and coordinating complex projects, which involves a mix of knowledge work and human interaction. gpt55_rationale: Architectural and engineering managers do largely cognitive and coordination-heavy work: planning projects, setting budgets and schedules, reviewing technical output, communicating with teams, and managing documentation, all of which AI tools can substantially accelerate. Demand could expand somewhat as cheaper engineering and design workflows enable more R&D, infrastructure, and product-development activity, but it is constrained by capital budgets, regulation, construction timelines, and the need for real-world implementation. The result is substantial restructuring: managers will oversee more AI-augmented workflows and larger spans of technical output, while those who cannot adapt to AI-enabled planning, analysis, and supervision may be displaced.

openai_rationale: The role of archivists, curators, and museum workers involves a mix of digital and physical tasks, such as cataloging and preserving documents, which AI can assist with but not fully automate. AI can enhance the management of electronic records and improve cataloging efficiency, but the hands-on work of preserving and displaying artifacts remains largely manual. gpt55_rationale: AI can materially assist with archival description, metadata generation, OCR/transcription, search, provenance research, exhibit text, grant writing, and digital records management. Demand could expand moderately because many archives and museums have large backlogs of uncataloged or undigitized materials, but budgets, physical collections, and public funding constraints limit how much cheaper output translates into more jobs. opus_rationale: Art direction is predominantly digital, conceptual, and visual work — much of it (mood boards, layout drafts, image generation, design iteration) is directly in the path of generative AI tools that already materially change creative workflows, driving a high disruption score. However, the core role blends client communication, creative vision, leadership, and final judgment that AI augments rather than replaces. Demand for visual content is highly elastic: as production becomes cheaper and faster, businesses, media, and individuals consume far more visual output across web, video, advertising, and packaging, unlocking latent demand. With disruption >=7 and elasticity >=7, art directors fit augment — each director orchestrates AI-assisted output to produce dramatically more, keeping headcount stable to growing.
openai_rationale: Art directors' work is predominantly knowledge-based, involving creative decision-making, visual design, and team management, which are increasingly supported by AI tools. gpt55_rationale: Art directors do largely cognitive, digital, and creative work—concept development, visual selection, layout/style direction, client presentation, and review of design output—which is directly affected by generative image, video, layout, and branding tools. openai_rationale: Assemblers and fabricators primarily engage in physical tasks such as assembling parts and conducting quality checks, which are less susceptible to AI disruption. While automation and robotics are increasingly used, the core tasks still require human dexterity and physical presence, leading to a low disruption score. Demand elasticity is low because the need for assembled products is not significantly suppressed by current costs or speed; thus, productivity gains from AI and automation are unlikely to result in a proportional increase in demand. gpt55_rationale: Assemblers and fabricators do mostly physical, hands-on work involving positioning parts, using tools, soldering, welding, fitting, and performing in-person quality checks, so generative AI affects only limited schematic-reading, inspection, training, and workflow-support tasks. Demand elasticity is low-to-moderate because cheaper assembly may support some reshoring and growth in areas such as EV batteries or electronics, but demand for vehicles, appliances, machinery, and fabricated products is ultimately constrained by final-product demand and capital investment. title: Athletes and sports competitors

opus_rationale: The core work of professional athletes is inherently physical, requiring human athleticism, hand-eye coordination, stamina, and real-time competition that AI cannot perform or replace. AI touches only peripheral activities like performance analysis, opponent scouting, and injury prevention, leaving the actual competing entirely human. Demand is highly constrained by the fixed number of league roster spots and the rarity of franchise expansion, so even cheaper training tools would not expand headcount substantially. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient to AI.
openai_rationale: The core tasks of athletes and sports competitors are highly physical and require real-world presence, making AI disruption minimal. opus_rationale: Athletic training is overwhelmingly hands-on physical work — applying tape and braces, providing on-field emergency care, manual rehabilitation, and real-time injury evaluation requiring physical presence. AI touches only peripheral tasks like record-keeping, report writing, and possibly diagnostic support, leaving the physical core untouched. Demand is moderately elastic given growing sports participation and aging active adults, but the work itself is not gated by cost of cognitive tasks. With disruption well below 7, this occupation is resilient: AI augments documentation but does not reshape the core hands-on work.
openai_rationale: Athletic trainers perform a mix of physical and cognitive tasks, such as applying protective devices and evaluating injuries, which require human presence and judgment. AI may assist with administrative tasks and data analysis but cannot replace the hands-on, empathetic care required. title: Atmospheric scientists, including meteorologists
claude_rationale: Atmospheric science involves significant computational modeling and data analysis that AI can enhance, but core work requires domain expertise in interpreting complex atmospheric phenomena, field data collection, and real-time decision-making during severe weather events. While AI tools can improve forecasting models and automate some data processing, the profession demands deep scientific understanding and human judgment for critical weather warnings. Demand elasticity is low because weather forecasting needs are relatively fixed - businesses and the public don't consume dramatically more weather services just because they're cheaper or faster, and much employment depends on government funding with structural constraints.

The forecasting and modeling core can be heavily automated while human roles shift toward model oversight, interpretation, severe-weather decision-making, client-specific analysis, broadcast communication, and forensic/research work. gpt55_rationale: Atmospheric science is heavily data-, model-, code-, graphics-, and communication-based, and AI is already improving forecasting, nowcasting, climate modeling, report drafting, and visualization. openai_rationale: Automotive service technicians and mechanics perform a mix of physical and cognitive tasks, with a significant portion involving hands-on repair and maintenance that AI cannot easily automate. openai_rationale: Baking is predominantly a physical and manual occupation, involving tasks like kneading dough, shaping pastries, and monitoring baking processes, which are not easily automated by AI. opus_rationale: The work is almost entirely digital and language-based — phone negotiations, skip tracing via databases, record updating, and applying scripted legal disclosures — all squarely in the path of AI voice agents, automated dialers, and NLP-driven negotiation tools.
